changes.summary: In the context of the exhibitions devoted to acquisitions held in celebration of the Musée d'Orsay’s 40th birthday, a new selection highlights works emblematic of the artistic renewal of the 1890s. During those years, sculptors and ceramists, fascinated by the possibilities provided by faïence, porcelain and sandstone, pushed the boundaries of their art. In the 1890s, the renewal of sculpture aligned with practitioners’ interest in creating new forms of ceramics and glassware. In turn, the effects of materials and colors discovered by ceramists won over sculptors, who were giving ever greater thought to their works’ polychromy. Faïence, porcelain and sandstone – these three materials produced from clayey soils were mediums for original creations. Influenced by Japanese stoneware, Chinese monochrome porcelains, iridescent Islamic ceramics and European vernacular pottery traditions, sculptors and ceramists gave expression to a variety of sensibilities and called the utilitarian limits of these techniques into question. The theme of the mask has been a genre in its own right since the 1860s. The Musée d’Orsay’s collection is a benchmark in this field and has recently been enriched with two striking examples testifying to the diversity of their creators’ approaches.
